inline.s: In the Ming dynasty there was a man of Ehu named Fei Hong. Once, while playing chess with a friend who had ranked with him in the same year’s examination, the two contended against each other and Fei Hong jokingly slapped his friend, who was displeased. Fei Hong deeply regretted it and went to his friend’s house every day to beg forgiveness, yet his friend would never come out to meet him. When Fei Hong’s father learned of this he was angry, sealed up a bamboo board, and sent a man to deliver it to the capital, instructing Fei Hong to strike himself with it. Fei Hong then took his father’s letter and the bamboo board to his friend’s house and flogged himself three times; only then did the friend come out to meet him, and the two threw their arms about each other and wept. Fei Hong said: ‘This is the wrong I committed—why are you weeping too?’ The friend said: ‘You still have a father to urge and reprove you, while I can no longer find even one to urge and reprove me!’ From that time on the two were as affectionate as before.

From this we may see that even after his father had passed away he was still moved to grief over such a matter—so we know that while his father was living he could never have had the heart to offend him. Yet today, although many fathers are still alive, the time we share with them is not necessarily long! The brevity of life and the certainty of parting, when we reflect on them, wrench the heart. How can we fail to be filial, respectful, and reverent?

Cui Xiaowei, a man of the Later Wei, served his elder brother Xiaofen with great reverence and gentleness; in sitting, standing, advancing, and withdrawing, he followed his elder brother’s commands in everything. Not a single coin or a foot of cloth did he ever take into his own private stores, and the women of the household too loved one another—a situation rarely to be seen in the world today!

The Ming scholar Yan Maoyou said: ‘People today are unfilial to their parents simply because they are unwilling to search their hearts and reflect. Consider only this: where does your body come from? Where will your parents go in the end? Since the new branches and leaves have already grown forth, the old root is about to wither! We use only the most ordinary food and drink to support our parents and make them glad—how can that repay so much as one ten-thousandth of their kindness? If we think in this way often, the filial heart will naturally arise.’ He also said: ‘People today do not honor their elder brothers simply because they are unwilling to turn the mind back and ask themselves. Just think of the vast and boundless universe—how short a time since I came into being! And in the boundless sea of humanity, how many are truly one’s own blood brothers? Grown up together in childhood, playing together, in old age we ought to support one another; so the affection between brothers naturally becomes sincere. If people would but take these two stories of Fei Hong and Cui Xiaowei, together with the words of Mr. Yan, and read and ponder them deeply, they would naturally be moved to tears streaming down both cheeks, and their true nature of filial piety and fraternal love would be set fully before them. So why need the retributions for offending one’s father and elder brother be listed again?’
The Most High’s Tract on Actions and Responses: A Vernacular Abridgment of Collected Annotations, Lectures, and Verified Cases, Volume Three — End
